arXiv:1504.07251v2 [quant-ph] 09 Jun 2015

Universal recovery map for approximate Markov chains

UMR 5668 LIP - ENS Lyon - CNRS - UCBL - INRIA, UniversitéÂ de Lyon
David Sutter Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich, Switzerland    Omar Fawzi Affiliation: Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech, USA Affiliation: LIP, ENS de Lyon, France    Renato Renner Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich, Switzerland
Abstract

A Markov chain is a tripartite quantum state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} whose CC-part can be recovered from the BB-part only, i.e., there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that ρA​B​C=ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B)\rho_{ABC}=\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}). More generally, an approximate Markov chain ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} is a state whose distance to the closest recovered state ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}) is small. As proved recently in [Fawzi and Renner, arXiv:1410.0664], this distance can be bounded from above by the conditional mutual information I(A:C|B)I(A\!:\!C|B) of the state. While the proof is non-constructive, one may expect that the recovery is universal, in the sense that the same map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} works for all states with a given marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC}. Here we show that this is indeed the case.

1 Introduction

A state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on a tripartite quantum system A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C forms a (quantum) Markov chain if it can be recovered from its marginal ρA​B\rho_{AB} on A⊗BA\otimes B by a quantum operation ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} from BB to B⊗CB\otimes C, i.e.,

ρA​B​C=ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B).\displaystyle\rho_{ABC}=\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\ . (1)

An equivalent characterization of ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} being a Markov chain is that the conditional mutual information I(A:C|B)ρ:=H(AB)ρ+H(BC)ρ−H(B)ρ−H(ABC)ρI(A:C|B)_{\rho}:=H(AB)_{\rho}+H(BC)_{\rho}-H(B)_{\rho}-H(ABC)_{\rho} is zero [21, 24, 25] where H​(A)ρ:=−tr⁡(ρA​log2​ρA)H(A)_{\rho}:=-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{A}\log_{2}\rho_{A}) is the von Neumann entropy. The structure of these states has been studied in various works. In particular, it has been shown that AA and CC can be viewed as independent conditioned on BB, for a meaningful notion of conditioning [16]. Very recently it has been shown that Markov states can be alternatively characterized by having a generalized Rényi conditional mutual information that vanishes [9].

A natural question that is relevant for applications is whether the above statements are robust (see [20] for an example and [11] for a discussion). Specifically, one would like to have a characterization of the states that have a small (but not necessarily vanishing) conditional mutual information, i.e., I(A:C|B)≤ε{I(A:C|B)}\leq\varepsilon for ε>0\varepsilon>0. First results revealed that such states can have a large distance to Markov chains that is independent of ε\varepsilon [8, 19], which has been taken as an indication that their characterization may be difficult. However, it has subsequently been realized that a more appropriate measure instead of the distance to a (perfect) Markov chain is to consider how well (1) is satisfied [35, 20, 36, 4]. This motivated the definition of approximate Markov chains as states where (1) approximately holds.

In recent work [11], it has been shown that the set of approximate Markov chains indeed coincides with the set of states with small conditional mutual information. In particular, the distance between the two terms in (1), which may be measured in terms of their fidelity FF, is bounded by the conditional mutual information.11 1 The fidelity of ρ\rho and σ\sigma is defined as F⁡(ρ,σ):=‖ρ​σ‖1F(\rho,\sigma):=\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}\sqrt{\sigma}\right\rVert_{1}. More precisely, for any state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} there exists a trace-preserving completely positive map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} (the recovery map) such that

I(A:C|B)ρ≥−2log2F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)).\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq-2\log_{2}F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ . (2)

Furthermore, it can be shown that a converse inequality holds that is of the form I(A:C|B)ρ2≤−c2log2F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))I(A:C|B)^{2}_{\rho}\leq-c^{2}\log_{2}F(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})), where cc depends logarithmically on the dimension of AA [4, 11].

We also note that the fidelity term in (2), maximized over all recovery maps, i.e.,

F​(A;C|B)ρ:=supℛB→B​CF⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))\displaystyle F(A;C|B)_{\rho}:=\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}}F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ (3)

is called fidelity of recovery,22 2 We note that if AA, BB, and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces the supremum is achieved, since the set of recovery maps is compact (see Remark C.3) and the fidelity is continuous in the input state (see Lemma B.9 in [11]). and has been introduced and studied in [27, 5]. With this quantity the main result of [11] can be written as

I(A:C|B)ρ≥−2log2F(A;C|B)ρ.\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq-2\log_{2}F(A;C|B)_{\rho}\ . (4)

The fidelity of recovery has several natural properties, e.g., it is monotonous under local operations on AA and CC, and it is multiplicative [5].

The result of [11] has been extended in various ways. Based on quantum state redistribution protocols, it has been shown in [7] that (2) still holds if the fidelity term is replaced by the measured relative entropy33 3 The measured relative entropy is defined in Appendix B (Definition B.1). D𝕄​(⋅,⋅)D_{\mathbb{M}}(\cdot,\cdot), which is generally larger, i.e.,

I(A:C|B)ρ≥D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))≥−2log2F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)).\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\geq-2\log_{2}F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ . (5)

Furthermore, in [5] an alternative proof of (2) has been derived that uses properties of the fidelity of recovery (in particular, multiplicativity). Another recent work [3] showed how to generalize ideas from [11] to prove a remainder term for the monotonicity of the relative entropy in terms of a recovery map that satisfies (2).

All known proofs of (2) are non-constructive, in the sense that the recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} is not given explicitly. It is merely known [11] that if AA, BB, and CC are finite-dimensional then ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} can always be chosen such that it has the form

XB↦VB​C​ρB​C12​(ρB−12​UB​XB​UB†​ρB−12⊗idC)​ρB​C12​VB​C†\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto V_{BC}\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}U_{B}X_{B}U_{B}^{\dagger}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}V_{BC}^{\dagger} (6)

on the support of ρB\rho_{B}, where UBU_{B} and VB​CV_{BC} are unitaries on BB and B⊗CB\otimes C, respectively. It would be natural to expect that the choice of the recovery map that satisfies (2) only depends on ρB​C\rho_{BC}, however this is only known in special cases. One such special case are Markov chains ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, i.e., states for which (1) holds perfectly. Here a map of the form (6) with VB​C=idB​CV_{BC}=\mathrm{id}_{BC} and UB=idBU_{B}=\mathrm{id}_{B} (sometimes referred to as transpose map or Petz recovery map) serves as a perfect recovery map [24, 25]. Another case where a recovery map that only depends on ρB​C\rho_{BC} is known explicitly are states with a classical BB system, i.e., qcq-states of the form ρA​B​C=∑bPB​(b)​|b⟩​⟨b|⊗ρA​C,b\rho_{ABC}=\sum_{b}P_{B}(b)|b\rangle\!\langle b|\otimes\rho_{AC,b}, where PBP_{B} is a probability distribution, {|b⟩}b\{|b\rangle\}_{b} an orthonormal basis on BB and {ρA​C,b}b\{\rho_{AC,b}\}_{b} a family of states on A⊗CA\otimes C. As discussed in [11], for such states (2) holds for the recovery map defined by ℛB→B​C​(|b⟩​⟨b|)=|b⟩​⟨b|⊗ρC,b\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(|b\rangle\!\langle b|)=|b\rangle\!\langle b|\otimes\rho_{C,b} for all bb, where ρC,b=trA​(ρA​C,b)\rho_{C,b}=\mathrm{tr}_{A}(\rho_{AC,b}). For general states, however, the previous results left open the possibility that the recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} depends on the full state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} rather than the marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} only. In particular, the unitaries UBU_{B} and VB​CV_{BC} in (6), although acting only on BB respectively B⊗CB\otimes C, could have such a dependence.

In this work we show that for any state ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} that is universal—in the sense that the distance between any extension ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} of ρB​C\rho_{BC} and ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}) is bounded from above by the conditional mutual information I(A:C|B)ρI(A:C|B)_{\rho}. In other words we show that (2) remains valid if the recovery map is chosen depending on ρB​C\rho_{BC} only, rather than on ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}.

2 Main result

Theorem 2.1.

For any density operator ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C there exists a trace-preserving completely positive map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that for any extension ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C

I(A:C|B)ρ≥−2log2F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)),\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq-2\log_{2}F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ , (7)

where AA, BB, and CC are separable Hilbert spaces.

Remark 2.2.

If BB and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the statement of Theorem 2.1 can be tightened to

I(A:C|B)ρ≥D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)).\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\geq D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ . (8)
Remark 2.3.

The recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} predicted by Theorem 2.1 has the property that it maps ρB\rho_{B} to ρB​C\rho_{BC}. To see this, note that I(A:C|B)ρ~=0I(A:C|B)_{\tilde{\rho}}=0 for any density operator of the form ρ~A​B​C=ρA⊗ρB​C\tilde{\rho}_{ABC}=\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}. Theorem 2.1 thus asserts that ρ~A​B​C\tilde{\rho}_{ABC} must be equal to ℛB→B​C​(ρ~A​B)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\tilde{\rho}_{AB}), which implies that ρB​C=ℛB→B​C​(ρB)\rho_{BC}=\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{B}). We note that so far it was unknown whether recovery maps that satisfy (2) and have this property do exist.

We note that Theorem 2.1 does not reveal any information about the structure of the recovery map that satisfies (7). However, if we consider a linearized version of the bound (7), we can make more specific statements.

Corollary 2.4.

For any density operator ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C there exists a trace-preserving completely positive map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that for any extension ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C

F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))≥1−ln⁡(2)2I(A:C|B)ρ,\displaystyle F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\geq 1-\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\ , (9)

where AA, BB, and CC are separable Hilbert spaces. Furthermore, if BB and CC are finite-dimensional then ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} has the form

XB↦ρB​C12​𝒰B​C→B​C​(ρB−12​XB​ρB−12⊗idC)​ρB​C12\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathcal{U}_{BC\to BC}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}X_{B}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})\,\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}} (10)

on the support of ρB\rho_{B}, where 𝒰B​C→B​C\mathcal{U}_{BC\to BC} is a unital trace-preserving map from B⊗CB\otimes C to B⊗CB\otimes C.

Remark 2.5.

Following the proof of Corollary 2.4 we can deduce a more specific structure of the universal recovery map. In the finite-dimensional case the map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} satisfying (9) can be assumed to have the form

XB↦∫VB​CsρB​C12(ρB−12UBsXBUBs†ρB−12⊗idC)ρB​C12VB​Cs†μ(ds),\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto\int V^{s}_{BC}\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}U^{s}_{B}X_{B}U^{s\,\dagger}_{B}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}{V^{s\,\dagger}_{BC}}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}s)\ , (11)

where μ\mu is a probability measure on some set 𝒮\mathcal{S}, {VB​Cs}s∈𝒮\{V^{s}_{BC}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}} is a family of unitaries on B⊗CB\otimes C that commute with ρB​C\rho_{BC}, and {UBs}s∈𝒮\{U^{s}_{B}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}} is a family of unitaries on BB that commute with ρB\rho_{B}. However, the representation of the recovery map given in (10) has certain advantages compared to the representation (11). The fidelity maximized over all recovery maps of the form (10) can be phrased as a semidefinite program and therefore be computed efficiently, whereas it is unknown whether the same is possible for (11).

We note that for almost all density operators ρB​C\rho_{BC}, i.e., for all ρB​C\rho_{BC} except for a set of measure zero, we can replace the unitaries UBsU_{B}^{s} and VB​CsV_{BC}^{s} by complex matrix exponentials of the form ρBi​t\rho_{B}^{\mathrm{i}t} and ρB​Ci​t\rho_{BC}^{\mathrm{i}t}, respectively, with t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. This shows that (11) without the integral (the integration in (11) is only necessary to guarantee that the recovery map is universal) coincides with the recovery map found in [32].44 4 This follows by the equidistribution theorem which is a special case of the strong ergodic theorem [26, Section II.5] (see also [10]).

Example 2.6.

For density operators with a marginal on B⊗CB\otimes C of the form ρB​C=ρB⊗ρC\rho_{BC}=\rho_{B}\otimes\rho_{C}, a universal recovery map that satisfies (8) is uniquely defined on the support of ρB\rho_{B}—it is the transpose map, which in this case simplifies to ℛB→B​C:XB↦XB⊗ρC\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}:X_{B}\mapsto X_{B}\otimes\rho_{C}. It is straightforward to see that (8) holds. In fact, we even have equality if we consider the relative entropy (which is in general larger than the measured relative entropy), i.e.,

I(A:C|B)ρ=D(ρA​B​C||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)).\displaystyle I(A:C|B)_{\rho}=D\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ . (12)

The uniqueness of ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} on the support of ρB\rho_{B} follows by using the fact that the universal recovery map should perfectly recover the Markov state ρA​B⊗ρC\rho_{AB}\otimes\rho_{C} where ρA​B\rho_{AB} is a purification of ρB\rho_{B}. This forces ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} to agree with the transpose map on the support of ρB\rho_{B} [24, 25].

The proof of Theorem 2.1 is structured into two parts. We first prove the statement for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces BB, and CC in Section 3 and then show that this implies the statement for general separable Hilbert spaces in Section 4. The proof of Corollary 2.4 is given in Section 5.

3 Proof for finite dimensions

Throughout this section we assume that the Hilbert spaces BB and CC are finite-dimensional. In the proof Steps 1 - 3 below, we also make the same assumption for AA, but then drop it in Step 4. We start by explaining why (8) is a tightened version of (7) which was noticed in [7]. Let Dα(⋅||⋅)D_{\alpha}(\cdot|\hskip-1.13809pt|\cdot) be the α\alpha-Quantum Rényi Divergence as defined in [22, 33] with D1(ρ||σ)=D(ρ||σ):=tr(ρ(logρ−logσ))D_{1}(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma)=D(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma):=\mathrm{tr}(\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)). By definition of the measured relative entropy (see Definition B.1) we find for any two states ρ\rho and σ\sigma

D𝕄(ρ||σ)=supℳ∈𝕄D(ℳ(ρ)||ℳ(σ))≥supℳ∈𝕄D12(ℳ(ρ)||ℳ(σ))=−2log2infℳ∈𝕄F(ℳ(ρ),ℳ(σ))=−2​log2⁡F⁡(ρ,σ),D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma)=\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}D\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho)|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}(\sigma)\bigr)\geq\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}D_{\frac{1}{2}}\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho)|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}(\sigma)\bigr)=-2\log_{2}\inf_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}F\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho),\mathcal{M}(\sigma)\bigr)\\ =-2\log_{2}F(\rho,\sigma)\ , (13)

where 𝕄:={ℳ:ℳ⁡(ρ)=∑xtr⁡(ρ​Mx)​|x⟩​⟨x|​ with ​∑xMx=id}\mathbb{M}:=\{\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{M}(\rho)=\sum_{x}\mathrm{tr}(\rho M_{x})|x\rangle\!\langle x|\text{ with }\sum_{x}M_{x}=\mathrm{id}\} and {|x⟩}\{|x\rangle\} is a family of orthonormal vectors. The inequality step uses that α↦Dα(ρ||σ)\alpha\mapsto D_{\alpha}(\rho|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma) is a monotonically non-decreasing function in α\alpha [22, Theorem 7] and the final step follows from the fact that for any two states there exists an optimal measurement that does not increase their fidelity [13, Section 3.3]. As a result, in order to prove Theorem 2.1 for finite-dimensional BB and CC it suffices to prove (8).

We first derive a proposition (Proposition 3.1 below) and then show how it can be used to prove (8) (and, hence, Theorem 2.1). The proposition refers to a family of functions

D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)∋ρ↦Δℛ​(ρ)∈ℝ∪{−∞},\displaystyle\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\ni\rho\mapsto\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\ , (14)

parameterized by recovery maps ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C), where TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) denotes the set of trace-preserving completely positive maps from BB to B⊗CB\otimes C and D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C) denotes the set of density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C. Subsequently in the proof, the function family Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) will be constructed as the difference of the two terms in (8) (see Equation (50)) such that Δℛ​(ρ)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0 corresponds to (8). The proposition asserts that if for any extension ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} of ρB​C\rho_{BC} we have Δℛ​(ρ)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0 for some ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) and provided the function family Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) satisfies certain properties described below, then there exists a single recovery map ℛ\mathcal{R} for which Δℛ​(ρ)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0 for all extensions ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} of ρB​C\rho_{BC} on a fixed AA system. We note that the precise form of the function family Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) is irrelevant for Proposition 3.1 as long as it satisfies a list of properties as stated below.

As described above, our goal is to prove that there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that Δℛ​(ρ)≥0{\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0} for all ρA​B​C∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C) with a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C. To formulate our argument more concisely, we introduce some notation. For any set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of density operators ρA​B​C∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C) we define

Δℛ​(𝒮):=infρ∈𝒮Δℛ​(ρ).\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S}):=\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\ . (15)

The desired statement then reads as Δℛ​(𝒮)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0, for any set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of states on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC}. Furthermore, for any fixed states ρA​B​C0\rho^{0}_{ABC} and ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C and p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], we define

ρA^​A​B​Cp:=(1−p)​|0⟩​⟨0|A^⊗ρA​B​C0+p|1⟩​⟨1|A^⊗ρA​B​C,\displaystyle\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}ABC}:=(1-p)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|_{\hat{A}}\otimes\rho^{0}_{ABC}+p|1\rangle\!\langle 1|_{\hat{A}}\otimes\rho_{ABC}\ , (16)

where A^\hat{A} is an additional system with two orthogonal states |0⟩|0\rangle and |1⟩|1\rangle. More generally, for any fixed state ρA​B​C0\rho^{0}_{ABC} and for any set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of density operators ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} we set

𝒮p:={ρA^​A​B​Cp:ρA​B​C∈𝒮}.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{p}:=\bigl\{\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}ABC}:\,\rho_{ABC}\in\mathcal{S}\bigr\}\ . (17)
Required properties of the Δ\Delta-function.
  1. 1.

    For any ρA​B​C0,ρA​B​C∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho^{0}_{ABC},\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C) with identical marginals ρB​C0=ρB​C\rho^{0}_{BC}=\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C, for any ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C), and for any p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] we have Δℛ​(ρp)=(1−p)​Δℛ​(ρ0)+p​Δℛ​(ρ)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{p})=(1-p)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{0})+p\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho).

  2. 2.

    For any ℛ,ℛ′∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C), for any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], and ℛ¯=α​ℛ+(1−α)​ℛ′\bar{\mathcal{R}}=\alpha\mathcal{R}+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}^{\prime} we have Δℛ¯​(ρ)≥α​Δℛ​(ρ)+(1−α)​Δℛ′​(ρ)\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho)\geq\alpha\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)+(1-\alpha)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}(\rho) for all ρ∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C).

  3. 3.

    For any ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C), the function D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)∋ρ↦Δℛ​(ρ)∈ℝ∪{−∞}\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\ni\rho\mapsto\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} is upper semicontinuous.

  4. 4.

    For any ρ∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C), the function TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)∋ℛ↦Δℛ​(ρ)∈ℝ∪{−∞}\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C)\ni\mathcal{R}\mapsto\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} is upper semicontinuous.

Property 1 implies that for any state ρA​B​C0\rho^{0}_{ABC}, for any set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of operators ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} with ρB​C=ρB​C0\rho_{BC}=\rho^{0}_{BC}, and for any p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] we have

Δℛ​(𝒮p)=infρ∈𝒮Δℛ​(ρp)=(1−p)​Δℛ​(ρ0)+p​infρ∈𝒮Δℛ​(ρ)=(1−p)​Δℛ​(ρ0)+p​Δℛ​(𝒮).\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S}^{p})=\inf\limits_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{p})=(1-p)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{0})+p\inf\limits_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)=(1-p)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{0})+p\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})\ . (18)

Similarly, Property 2 implies

Δℛ¯​(𝒮)=infρ∈𝒮Δℛ¯​(ρ)≥infρ∈𝒮{α​Δℛ​(ρ)+(1−α)​Δℛ′​(ρ)}≥α​infρ∈𝒮Δℛ​(ρ)+(1−α)​infρ∈𝒮Δℛ′​(ρ)=α​Δℛ​(𝒮)+(1−α)​Δℛ′​(𝒮).\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S})=\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho)\geq\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\bigl\{\alpha\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)+(1-\alpha)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}(\rho)\bigr\}\\ \geq\alpha\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)+(1-\alpha)\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}(\rho)=\alpha\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})+(1-\alpha)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}(\mathcal{S})\ . (19)
Proposition 3.1.

Let AA, BB, and CC be finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, 𝒫⊆TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) be compact and convex, 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a set of density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with identical marginals on B⊗CB\otimes C, and Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) be a family of functions of the form (14) that satisfies Properties 1-4. Then

∀ρ∈𝒮​∃ℛ∈𝒫:Δℛ​(ρ)≥0⟹∃ℛ¯∈𝒫:Δℛ¯​(𝒮)≥0.\displaystyle\forall\rho\in\mathcal{S}\,\,\exists\mathcal{R}\in\mathcal{P}\ :\ \Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0\quad\implies\quad\exists\bar{\mathcal{R}}\in\mathcal{P}\ :\ \Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0\ . (20)

We now proceed in four steps. In the first, we prove Proposition 3.1 for finite sets 𝒮\mathcal{S}. This is done by induction over the cardinality of the set 𝒮\mathcal{S}. We show that if the statement of Proposition 3.1 is true for all sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} with |𝒮|=n|\mathcal{S}|=n, this implies that it remains valid for all sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} with |𝒮|=n+1|\mathcal{S}|=n+1. In Step 2, we use an approximation step to extend this to infinite sets 𝒮\mathcal{S} which then completes the proof of Proposition 3.1. In the final two steps, we show how to conclude the statement of Theorem 2.1 for the finite-dimensional case from that. In Step 3 we prove (8) for the case where the recovery map that satisfies (8) could still depend on the dimension of the system AA. In Step 4 we show how this dependency can be removed.

Step 1: Proof of Proposition 3.1 for finite size sets 𝒮\mathcal{S}

We proceed by induction over the cardinality n:=|𝒮|n:=|\mathcal{S}| of the set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of density operators. More precisely, the induction hypothesis is that for any finite-dimensional Hilbert space AA and any set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of size nn consisting of density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C, the statement (20) holds. For n=1n=1, this hypothesis holds trivially for ℛ¯=ℛ\bar{\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{R}.55 5 For n=0n=0, we have Δℛ​(𝒮)=∞≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})=\infty\geq 0 for any ℛ∈𝒫\mathcal{R}\in\mathcal{P} since the infimum of an empty set is infinity.

We now prove the induction step. Suppose that the induction hypothesis holds for some nn. Let AA be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let 𝒮∪{ρA​B​C0}\mathcal{S}\cup\{\rho_{ABC}^{0}\} be a set of cardinality n+1n+1 where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a set of states on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C of cardinality nn and ρA​B​C0\rho^{0}_{ABC} is another state with ρB​C0=ρB​C\rho^{0}_{BC}=\rho_{BC}. We need to prove that there exists a recovery map ℛ¯B→B​C∈𝒫\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{B\to BC}\in\mathcal{P} such that

Δℛ¯​(𝒮∪{ρA​B​C0})≥0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S}\cup\{\rho_{ABC}^{0}\})\geq 0\ . (21)

Let p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] and consider the set 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{p} as defined in (17). In the following we view the states ρp\rho^{p} (see Equation (16)) in this set as tripartite states on (A^⊗A)⊗B⊗C(\hat{A}\otimes A)\otimes B\otimes C, i.e., we regard the system A^⊗A\hat{A}\otimes A as one (larger) system. The induction hypothesis applied to the extension space A^⊗A\hat{A}\otimes A and the set 𝒮p\mathcal{S}^{p} (of size nn) of states on (A^⊗A)⊗B⊗C(\hat{A}\otimes A)\otimes B\otimes C implies the existence of a map ℛB→B​Cp∈𝒫\mathcal{R}^{p}_{B\to BC}\in\mathcal{P} such that

Δℛp​(𝒮p)≥0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\mathcal{S}^{p})\geq 0\ . (22)

As by assumption the function D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)∋ρ↦Δℛp​(ρ)∈ℝ∪{−∞}\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\ni\rho\mapsto\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\rho)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} satisfies Property 1 (and hence also Equation (18)) we obtain

(1−p)​Δℛp​(ρ0)+p​Δℛp​(𝒮)≥0.\displaystyle(1-p)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\rho^{0})+p\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0\ . (23)

This implies that

Δℛp​(ρ0)≥0orΔℛp​(𝒮)≥0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\rho^{0})\geq 0\quad\textnormal{or}\quad\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0\ . (24)

Furthermore, for p=0p=0 the left inequality holds and for p=1p=1 the right inequality holds. By choosing K0={p∈[0,1]:Δℛp​(ρ0)≥0}K_{0}=\{p\in[0,1]:\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\rho^{0})\geq 0\} and K1={p∈[0,1]:Δℛp​(𝒮)≥0}K_{1}=\{p\in[0,1]:\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{p}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0\}, Lemma D.1 implies that for any δ>0\delta>0 there exist u,v∈[0,1]u,v\in[0,1] with 0≤v−u≤δ0\leq v-u\leq\delta such that

Δℛu​(ρ0)≥0andΔℛv​(𝒮)≥0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{u}}(\rho^{0})\geq 0\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{v}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0\ . (25)

Note also that ℛB→B​Cu\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}^{u}, ℛB→B​Cv∈𝒫\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}^{v}\in\mathcal{P}, since by the induction hypothesis ℛB→B​Cp∈𝒫\mathcal{R}^{p}_{B\to BC}\in\mathcal{P} for any p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1].

We will use this to prove that the recovery map ℛ~∈𝒫\tilde{\mathcal{R}}\in\mathcal{P} defined by

ℛ~:=α​ℛu+(1−α)​ℛv,\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{R}}:=\alpha\mathcal{R}^{u}+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}^{v}\ , (26)

for an appropriately chosen α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], satisfies

Δℛ~​(ρ0)≥−c​δandΔℛ~​(𝒮)≥−c​δ,\displaystyle\Delta_{\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho^{0})\geq-c\delta\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\Delta_{\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S})\geq-c\delta\ , (27)

and thus proves (21).

(If v=1v=1 it suffices to consider the case α=1\alpha=1 so that the last term can be omitted; cf. Equation (41) below.) Analogously, using (19) and (35), we find

α​Λ0−(1−α)​v1−v​Λ1\displaystyle\alpha\Lambda^{0}-(1-\alpha)\frac{v}{1-v}\Lambda^{1} ≥−c​δ\displaystyle\geq-c\delta (39)

Step 2: Extension to infinite sets 𝒮\mathcal{S}

All that remains to be done to prove Proposition 3.1 is to generalize the statement to arbitrarily large sets 𝒮\mathcal{S}. In fact, we show that there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C∈𝒫\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}\in\mathcal{P} such that Δℛ​(𝒮)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of all density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C for a fixed finite-dimensional Hilbert space AA and a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC}.

Note first that this set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of all density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C is compact (see Lemma C.2). This implies that for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists a finite set 𝒮ε\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon} of density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C such that any ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} is ε\varepsilon-close to an element of 𝒮ε\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon}. We further assume without loss of generality that 𝒮ε′⊂𝒮ε\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\subset\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon} for ε′≥ε\varepsilon^{\prime}\geq\varepsilon. Let ℛε∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) be a map such that Δℛε​(𝒮ε)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}}(\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon})\geq 0, whose existence follows from the validity of Proposition 3.1 for sets of finite size (which we proved in Step 1). Since the set TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) is compact (see Remark C.3) there exists a decreasing sequence {εn}n∈ℕ\{\varepsilon_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} and ℛ¯∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\bar{\mathcal{R}}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) such that

limn→∞εn=0andℛ¯=limn→∞ℛεn.\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{n}=0\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\bar{\mathcal{R}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon_{n}}\ . (47)

Combining this with Property 4 gives for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}

Δℛ¯​(𝒮εn)=infρ∈𝒮εnΔℛ¯​(ρ)≥infρ∈𝒮εnlim supm→∞Δℛ¯εm​(ρ)≥lim supm→∞infρ∈𝒮εnΔℛ¯εm​(ρ)≥lim supm→∞infρ∈𝒮εmΔℛ¯εm​(ρ)=lim supm→∞Δℛεm​(𝒮εm)≥0,\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}})=\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}}}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho)\geq\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}}}\limsup_{m\to\infty}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}^{\varepsilon_{m}}}(\rho)\geq\limsup_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}}}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}^{\varepsilon_{m}}}(\rho)\\ \geq\limsup_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{m}}}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}^{\varepsilon_{m}}}(\rho)=\limsup_{m\to\infty}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon_{m}}}(\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{m}})\geq 0\ , (48)

where the third inequality holds since 𝒮εn⊂𝒮εm\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}}\subset\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{m}} for εn≥εm\varepsilon_{n}\geq\varepsilon_{m}, respectively n≤mn\leq m. The final inequality follows from the defining property of ℛε\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}. For any fixed ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} and for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, let ρn∈𝒮εn\rho^{n}\in\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}} be such that limn→∞ρn=ρ∈𝒮\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho^{n}=\rho\in\mathcal{S}. (By definition of 𝒮εn\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}} it follows that such a sequence {ρn}n∈ℕ\{\rho^{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} with ρn∈𝒮εn\rho^{n}\in\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}} always exists.) Property 3 together with (48) yields

Δℛ¯​(ρ)=Δℛ¯​(limn→∞ρn)≥lim supn→∞Δℛ¯​(ρn)≥lim supn→∞Δℛ¯​(𝒮εn)≥0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho)=\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho^{n})\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho^{n})\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S}^{\varepsilon_{n}})\geq 0\ . (49)

Since (49) holds for any ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S}, we obtain Δℛ¯​(𝒮)≥0\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0, which completes the proof of Proposition 3.1.

Step 3: From Proposition 3.1 to Theorem 2.1 for fixed system AA

We next show that Theorem 2.1, for the case where AA is a fixed finite-dimensional system, follows from Proposition 3.1. For this we use Proposition 3.1 for the function family

Δℛ:\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}:\,\,\,\, D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)→ℝ∪{−∞}\displaystyle\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}
ρA​B​C↦I(A:C|B)ρ−D𝕄(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)),\displaystyle\rho_{ABC}\mapsto I(A:C|B)_{\rho}-D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ , (50)

with ℛB→B​C∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C). We note that since CC is finite-dimensional this implies that Δℛ​(ρ)<∞\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)<\infty for all ρ∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C). To apply Proposition 3.1, we have to verify that the function family D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)∋ρ↦Δℛ​(ρ)∈ℝ∪{−∞}D(A\otimes B\otimes C)\ni\rho\mapsto\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} of the form (50) satisfies the assumptions of the proposition. This is ensured by the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

Let AA be a separable and BB and CC finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The function family Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) defined by (50) satisfies Properties 1-4.

Proof.

We first verify that the function Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) satisfies Property 1. For any state ρp\rho^{p} of the form (16), we have by the definition of the mutual information

I(A^A:C|B)ρp=H(C|B)ρp−H(C|BAA^)ρp.\displaystyle I(\hat{A}A:C|B)_{\rho^{p}}=H(C|B)_{\rho^{p}}-H(C|BA\hat{A})_{\rho^{p}}\ . (51)

Because ρB​C0=ρB​C\rho^{0}_{BC}=\rho_{BC}, the first term, H​(C|B)ρpH(C|B)_{\rho^{p}}, is independent of pp, i.e., H​(C|B)ρp=H​(C|B)ρ0=H​(C|B)ρH(C|B)_{\rho^{p}}=H(C|B)_{\rho^{0}}=H(C|B)_{\rho}. The second term can be written as an expectation over A^\hat{A}, i.e.,

H​(C|B​A​A^)ρp=(1−p)​H​(C|B​A)ρ0+p​H​(C|B​A)ρ.\displaystyle H(C|BA\hat{A})_{\rho^{p}}={(1-p)}H(C|BA)_{\rho^{0}}+pH(C|BA)_{\rho}\ . (52)

As a result we find

I(A^A:C|B)ρp=(1−p)I(A:C|B)ρ0+pI(A:C|B)ρ.\displaystyle I(\hat{A}A:C|B)_{\rho^{p}}=(1-p)I(A:C|B)_{\rho^{0}}+pI(A:C|B)_{\rho}\ . (53)

The density operator ℛB→B​C​(ρA^​A​Bp)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}AB}) can be written as

ℛB→B​C​(ρA^​A​Bp)=(1−p)​|0⟩​⟨0|A^⊗ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B0)+p|1⟩​⟨1|A^⊗ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B).\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}AB})=(1-p)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|_{\hat{A}}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho^{0}_{AB})+p|1\rangle\!\langle 1|_{\hat{A}}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\ . (54)

We can thus apply Lemma B.3, from which we obtain

D𝕄(ρA^​A​B​Cp||ℛB→B​C(ρA^​A​Bp))=(1−p)D𝕄(ρA​B​C0||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B0))+pD𝕄(ρA​B​Cp||ℛB→B​C(ρA​Bp)).\displaystyle D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{\hat{A}ABC}^{p}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{\hat{A}AB}^{p})\bigr)=(1-p)D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}^{0}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}^{0})\bigr)+pD_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}^{p}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}^{p})\bigr)\ . (55)

Equations (53) and (55) imply that

Δℛ​(ρp)=(1−p)​Δℛ​(ρ0)+p​Δℛ​(ρ),\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{p})=(1-p)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho^{0})+p\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\ , (56)

which concludes the proof of Property 1.

That Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) satisfies Property 2 can be seen as follows. Let ℛB→B​C,ℛB→B​C′∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC},\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C), α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] and ℛ¯B→B​C=α​ℛB→B​C+(1−α)​ℛB→B​C′\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{B\to BC}=\alpha\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC}. D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛ¯B→B​C(ρA​B))=D𝕄(ρA​B​C||αℛB→B​C(ρA​B)+(1−α)ℛ′B→B​C(ρA​B))≤αD𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))+(1−α)D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛ′B→B​C(ρA​B))D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)=D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\alpha\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\\ \leq\alpha D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)+(1-\alpha)D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr) (57)

and hence

Δℛ¯​(ρ)≥α​Δℛ​(ρ)+(1−α)​Δℛ′​(ρ).\displaystyle\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho)\geq\alpha\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)+(1-\alpha)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}(\rho)\ . (58)

We next verify that the function Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) satisfies Property 3. The Alicki-Fannes inequality ensures that D(A⊗B⊗C)∋ρ↦I(A:C|B)ρ∈ℝ+\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\ni\rho\mapsto{I(A:C|B)_{\rho}}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is continuous since CC is finite-dimensional [1]. By the definition of Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) it thus suffices to show that D(A⊗B⊗C)∋ρA​B​C↦D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))∈ℝ+\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\ni\rho_{ABC}\mapsto D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}))\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is lower semicontinuous. Let {ρA​B​Cn}n∈ℕ\{\rho_{ABC}^{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of states on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C such that limn→∞ρA​B​Cn=ρA​B​C∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho_{ABC}^{n}=\rho_{ABC}\in{\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)}. By definition of the measured relative entropy (see Definition B.1), we find for 𝕄:={ℳ:ℳ⁡(ρ)=∑xtr⁡(ρ​Mx)​|x⟩​⟨x|​ with ​∑xMx=id}\mathbb{M}:=\{\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{M}(\rho)=\sum_{x}\mathrm{tr}(\rho M_{x})|x\rangle\!\langle x|\text{ with }\sum_{x}M_{x}=\mathrm{id}\},

lim infn→∞D𝕄(ρA​B​Cn||ℛB→B​C(ρA​Bn))\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}^{n}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}^{n})\bigr) =lim infn→∞supℳ∈𝕄D(ℳ(ρA​B​Cn)||ℳ(ℛB→B​C(ρA​Bn)))\displaystyle=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}D\Bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho_{ABC}^{n})|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}^{n})\bigr)\Bigr)
≥supℳ∈𝕄lim infn→∞D(ℳ(ρA​B​Cn)||ℳ(ℛB→B​C(ρA​Bn)))\displaystyle\geq\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}\liminf_{n\to\infty}D\Bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho_{ABC}^{n})|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}^{n})\bigr)\Bigr)
≥supℳ∈𝕄D(ℳ(ρA​B​C)||ℳ(ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)))\displaystyle\geq\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}D\Bigl(\mathcal{M}(\rho_{ABC})|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\Bigr)
=D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)).\displaystyle=D_{\mathbb{M}}\bigl(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\ . (59)

In the penultimate step, we use that the relative entropy is lower semicontinuous [18, Exercise 7.22] and that ℳ\mathcal{M} as well as ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} are linear and bounded operators and hence continuous.

We finally show that Δℛ​(⋅)\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) fulfills Property 4. It suffices to verify that TPCP(B,B⊗C)∋ℛ↦D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛ(ρA​B))∈ℝ+{\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C)}\ni\mathcal{R}\mapsto D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}(\rho_{AB}))\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is lower semicontinuous where by definition we have D𝕄(ρA​B​C||ℛ(ρA​B))=supℳ∈𝕄D(ℳ(ρA​B​C)||ℳ(ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)))D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{ABC}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{R}(\rho_{AB}))=\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{M}}D(\mathcal{M}(\rho_{ABC})|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}))). Note that since ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℳ\mathcal{M} are linear bounded operators and hence continuous and the relative entropy for two states σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} is defined by D(σ1||σ2):=tr(σ1(logσ1−logσ2))D(\sigma_{1}|\hskip-1.13809pt|\sigma_{2}):=\mathrm{tr}(\sigma_{1}(\log\sigma_{1}-\log\sigma_{2})) we find that ℛ↦D(ℳ(ρA​B​C)||ℳ(ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)))\mathcal{R}\mapsto D(\mathcal{M}(\rho_{ABC})|\hskip-1.13809pt|\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}))) is continuous as the logarithm ℝ+∋x↦log⁡x∈ℝ\mathbb{R}^{+}\ni x\mapsto\log x\in\mathbb{R} is continuous. Since the supremum of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous [6, Chapter IV, Section 6.2, Theorem 4], the assertion follows.

∎

What remains to be shown in order to apply Proposition 3.1 is that for any ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of states on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C, there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C∈𝒫\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}\in\mathcal{P} such that Δℛ​(ρ)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0. By choosing 𝒫=TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{P}=\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C), the main result of [7] however precisely proves this. We have thus shown that Δℛ​(ρ)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)\geq 0 holds for a universal recovery map ℛB→B​C∈𝒫\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}\in\mathcal{P}, so that (8) follows for any fixed dimension of the AA system. This proves the statement of Remark 2.2 (and, hence, Theorem 2.1) for the case where AA is a fixed finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

Step 4: Independence from the AA system

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the set of all density operators on A¯⊗B⊗C\bar{A}\otimes B\otimes C with a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C, where BB and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and A¯\bar{A} is the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space ℓ2\ell^{2} of square summable sequences. We now show that there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that Δℛ​(𝒮)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0.

Let {ΠA¯a}a∈ℕ\{\Pi_{\bar{A}}^{a}\}_{a\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of finite-rank projectors on A¯\bar{A} that converges to idA¯\mathrm{id}_{\bar{A}} with respect to the weak operator topology. Let 𝒮a\mathcal{S}^{a} denote the set of states whose marginal on A¯\bar{A} is contained in the support of ΠA¯a\Pi^{a}_{\bar{A}} and with the same fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C as the elements of 𝒮\mathcal{S}. For all a∈ℕa\in\mathbb{N}, let ℛB→B​Ca\mathcal{R}^{a}_{B\to BC} denote a recovery map that satisfies Δℛa​(𝒮a)≥0\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{a}}(\mathcal{S}^{a})\geq 0. Note that the existence of such maps is already established by the proof of Theorem 2.1 for the finite-dimensional case. As the set of trace-preserving completely positive maps on finite-dimensional systems is compact (see Remark C.3) there exists a subsequence {ai}i∈ℕ\{a_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} such that limi→∞ai=∞\lim_{i\to\infty}a_{i}=\infty and limi→∞ℛai=ℛ¯∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{R}^{a_{i}}=\bar{\mathcal{R}}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C). For every ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S} there exists a sequence of states {ρa}a∈ℕ\{\rho^{a}\}_{a\in\mathbb{N}} with ρa∈𝒮a\rho^{a}\in\mathcal{S}^{a} that converges to ρ\rho in the trace norm (see Lemma E.3). Lemma 3.2 (in particular Properties 3 and 4), yields for any ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S}

Δℛ¯​(ρ)≥lim supa→∞Δℛ¯​(ρa)≥lim supa→∞lim supi→∞Δℛai​(ρa)≥lim supa→∞lim supi→∞infρ∈𝒮aΔℛai​(ρ)≥lim supi→∞infρ∈𝒮aiΔℛai​(ρ)=lim supi→∞Δℛai​(𝒮ai)≥0.\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho)\geq\limsup_{a\to\infty}\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\rho^{a})\geq\limsup_{a\to\infty}\limsup_{i\to\infty}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{a_{i}}}(\rho^{a})\geq\limsup_{a\to\infty}\limsup_{i\to\infty}\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}^{a}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{a_{i}}}(\rho)\\ \geq\limsup_{i\to\infty}\inf_{\rho\in\mathcal{S}^{a_{i}}}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{a_{i}}}(\rho)=\limsup_{i\to\infty}\Delta_{\mathcal{R}^{a_{i}}}(\mathcal{S}^{a_{i}})\geq 0\ . (60)

The fourth inequality follows since ai≥aa_{i}\geq a for large enough ii and since this implies that 𝒮ai⊃𝒮a\mathcal{S}^{a_{i}}\supset\mathcal{S}^{a}, and the final inequality follows by definition of ℛai\mathcal{R}^{a_{i}}. This shows that Δℛ¯​(𝒮)≥0\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0.

To retrieve the statement of Remark 2.2 (and hence Theorem 2.1 for finite-dimensional BB and CC), we need to argue that this same map ℛ¯\bar{\mathcal{R}} remains valid when we consider any separable space AA. In order to do this, observe that any separable Hilbert space AA can be isometrically embedded into A¯\bar{A} [26, Theorem II.7]. To conclude, it suffices to remark that Δℛ¯\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}} is invariant under isometries applied on the space AA.

4 Extension to infinite dimensions

In this section we show how to obtain the statement of Theorem 2.1 for separable (not necessarily finite-dimensional) Hilbert spaces AA, BB, CC from the finite-dimensional case that has been proven in Section 3. For trace non-increasing completely positive maps ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} we define the function family

Δ¯ℛ:\displaystyle\bar{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}:\,\,\,\, D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)→ℝ∪{−∞}\displaystyle\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}
ρA​B​C↦F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))−2−12I(A:C|B)ρ,\displaystyle\rho_{ABC}\mapsto F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)-2^{-\frac{1}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}}\ , (61)

where D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C) denotes the set of states on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C. We will use the same notation as introduced at the beginning of Section 3. In addition, we take 𝒮\mathcal{S} to be the set of all states on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C. The proof proceeds in two steps where we first show that there exists a sequence of recovery maps {ℛB→B​Ck}k∈ℕ\{\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}^{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} such that limk→∞Δ¯ℛk​(𝒮)≥0\lim_{k\to\infty}\bar{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}^{k}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0, where the property that all elements of 𝒮\mathcal{S} have the same marginal on the B⊗CB\otimes C system will be important. In the second step we conclude by an approximation argument that there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that Δ¯ℛ​(𝒮)≥0\bar{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0.

Let {ΠBb}b∈ℕ\{\Pi_{B}^{b}\}_{b\in\mathbb{N}} and {ΠCc}c∈ℕ\{\Pi_{C}^{c}\}_{c\in\mathbb{N}} be sequences of finite-rank projectors on BB and CC which converge to idB\mathrm{id}_{B} and idC\mathrm{id}_{C} with respect to the weak operator topology. For any given ρA​B​C∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C) consider the normalized projected states

Step 2: Existence of a limit

Recall that 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of density operators on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C with a fixed marginal ρB​C\rho_{BC} on B⊗CB\otimes C. The goal of this step is to use (78) to prove that there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} such that

Δ¯ℛ​(𝒮)≥0.\displaystyle\bar{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S})\geq 0\ . (79)

Let {ΠBm}m∈ℕ\{\Pi_{B}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} and {ΠCm}m∈ℕ\{\Pi_{C}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} be sequences of projectors with rank mm that weakly converge to idB\mathrm{id}_{B} and idC\mathrm{id}_{C}, respectively. Furthermore, for any mm and any ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) let [ℛ]m[\mathcal{R}]^{m} be the trace non-increasing map obtained from ℛ\mathcal{R} by projecting the input and output with ΠBm\Pi_{B}^{m} and ΠBm⊗ΠCm\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}, respectively. We start with a preparatory lemma that proves a relation between Δ¯[ℛ]m​(𝒮)\bar{\Delta}_{[\mathcal{R}]^{m}}(\mathcal{S}) and Δ¯ℛ​(𝒮)\bar{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathcal{S}).

Lemma 4.2.

For any ρB​C∈D⁡(B⊗C)\rho_{BC}\in\mathrm{D}(B\otimes C) there exists a sequence of reals {δm}m∈ℕ\{\delta^{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} with limm→∞δm=0\lim_{m\to\infty}\delta^{m}=0,88 8 The precise form of the sequence {δm}m∈ℕ\{\delta^{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} can be found in the proof (see Equation (87)). such that for any ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) we have

where ‖ℛ⁡(ρB)−ρB​C‖1≤ε\left\lVert\mathcal{R}(\rho_{B})-\rho_{BC}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon.

Proof.

For any ρA​B​C∈𝒮\rho_{ABC}\in\mathcal{S} and any m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} let us define the non-negative operator ρ^A​Bm:=(idA⊗ΠBm)​ρA​B\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB}:={(\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\Pi_{B}^{m})}\rho_{AB} (idA⊗ΠBm){(\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\Pi_{B}^{m})}. we have F⁡(ρA​B​C,ρ~A​B​Cm)≥F⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))−δm−4​ε14F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\tilde{\rho}^{m}_{ABC}\bigr)\geq F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)-\delta^{m}-4\,\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}. Similarly, we obtain

(83)

By Hölder’s inequality, monotonicity of the trace norm for trace-preserving completely positive maps [31, Example 9.1.8 and Corollary 9.1.10] and (82) together with the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequality [12] and Lemma E.1 we find

|tr⁡((ℛB→B​C​(ρ^Bm)−ℛB→B​C​(ρB))​ΠBm⊗ΠCm)|≤‖ℛB→B​C​(ρB)−ℛB→B​C​(ρ^Bm)‖1​‖ΠBm⊗ΠCm‖∞=‖ℛB→B​C​(ρB)−ℛB→B​C​(ρ^Bm)‖1≤‖ρB−ρ^Bm‖1≤‖ρA​B−ρ^A​Bm‖1≤2​1−tr​(ρB​ΠBm)2.\left|\mathrm{tr}\Bigl(\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{B})-\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{B})\bigr)\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}\Bigr)\right|\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{B})-\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{B})\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}\right\rVert_{\infty}\\ =\left\lVert\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{B})-\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{B})\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert\rho_{B}-\hat{\rho}^{m}_{B}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert\rho_{AB}-\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 2\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})^{2}}\ . (84)

Combining (83), (84) and Hölder’s inequality together with the assumption ‖ℛ⁡(ρB)−ρB​C‖1≤ε\left\lVert\mathcal{R}(\rho_{B})-\rho_{BC}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon gives

P​(ℛB→B​C​(ρ^A​Bm),ρ~A​B​Cm)2\displaystyle P\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB}),\tilde{\rho}^{m}_{ABC}\bigr)^{2} ≤1−tr​(ℛB→B​C​(ρB)​ΠBm⊗ΠCm)2+4​1−tr​(ρB​ΠBm)2\displaystyle\leq 1-\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{B})\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}\bigr)^{2}+4\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})^{2}}
≤1−tr​(ρB​C​ΠBm⊗ΠCm)2+4​1−tr​(ρB​ΠBm)2+2​ε.\displaystyle\leq 1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{BC}\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m})^{2}+4\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})^{2}}+2\varepsilon\ . (85)

≤P⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))+P⁡(ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B),ℛB→B​C​(ρ^A​Bm))+P⁡(ℛB→B​C​(ρ^A​Bm),ρ~A​B​Cm)\displaystyle\hskip 11.38109pt\leq P\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)+P\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB}),\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB})\bigr)+P\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB}),\tilde{\rho}^{m}_{ABC}\bigr)
≤P⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))+P⁡(ρA​B,ρ^A​Bm)+P⁡(ℛB→B​C​(ρ^A​Bm),ρ~A​B​Cm)\displaystyle\hskip 11.38109pt\leq P\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)+P\bigl(\rho_{AB},\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB}\bigr)+P\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\hat{\rho}^{m}_{AB}),\tilde{\rho}^{m}_{ABC}\bigr)
≤P⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))+(δm)2/8+2​ε,\displaystyle\hskip 11.38109pt\leq P\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)+(\delta^{m})^{2}/8+\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\ , (86)

for

δm:=8​(1−tr​(ρB​ΠBm)2+1−tr​(ρB​C​ΠBm⊗ΠCm)2+4​1−tr​(ρB​ΠBm)2)12.\displaystyle\delta^{m}:=\sqrt{8}\left(\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})^{2}}+\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{BC}\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m})^{2}+4\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})^{2}}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\ . (87)

F​(ρA​B​C,ρ~A​B​Cm)2≥F​(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))2−(δm)2−8​2​ε≥(F⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))−(δm)2+8​2​ε)2.F(\rho_{ABC},\tilde{\rho}^{m}_{ABC})^{2}\geq F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)^{2}-(\delta^{m})^{2}-8\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\\ \geq\Bigl(F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)-\sqrt{(\delta^{m})^{2}+8\sqrt{2\varepsilon}}\Bigr)^{2}\ . (88)

As a result, we find

F⁡(ρA​B​C,ρ~A​B​Cm)≥F⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C​(ρA​B))−δm−8​(2​ε)14,\displaystyle F(\rho_{ABC},\tilde{\rho}^{m}_{ABC})\geq F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)-\delta^{m}-\sqrt{8}(2\varepsilon)^{\frac{1}{4}}\ , (89)

which proves (80) since 8​ 214≤4\sqrt{8}\,2^{\frac{1}{4}}\leq 4.

Recall that BB and CC are separable Hilbert spaces and that {ΠBm}m∈ℕ\{\Pi_{B}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} and {ΠBm⊗ΠCm}m∈ℕ\{\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} converge weakly to idB\mathrm{id}_{B} and idB⊗idC\mathrm{id}_{B}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C} respectively. Lemma E.2 thus shows that limm→∞tr⁡(ρB​ΠBm)=1\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{B}\,\Pi_{B}^{m})=1 and limm→∞tr⁡(ρB​C​ΠBm⊗ΠCm)=1\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathrm{tr}(\rho_{BC}{\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}})=1, which implies limm→∞δm=0\lim_{m\to\infty}\delta^{m}=0. ∎

The following lemma proves that for sufficiently large mm and a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} that maps ρB\rho_{B} to density operators that are close to ρB​C\rho_{BC}, the operator [ℛ]m​(ρA​B)[\mathcal{R}]^{m}(\rho_{AB}) has a trace that is bounded from below by essentially one.

Lemma 4.3.

Let AA, BB, and CC be separable Hilbert spaces. For any density operator ρA​B∈D⁡(A⊗B)\rho_{AB}\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B) and any ℛ∈TPCP⁡(B,B⊗C)\mathcal{R}\in\mathrm{TPCP}(B,B\otimes C) we have

tr⁡([ℛ]m​(ρA​B))≥tr⁡(ΠBm⊗ΠCm​ρB​C)−2​1−tr⁡(ΠBm​ρB)−‖ℛ⁡(ρB)−ρB​C‖1.\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}\bigl([\mathcal{R}]^{m}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\geq\mathrm{tr}(\Pi_{B}^{m}\otimes\Pi_{C}^{m}\rho_{BC})-2\sqrt{1-\mathrm{tr}(\Pi_{B}^{m}\rho_{B})}-\left\lVert\mathcal{R}(\rho_{B})-\rho_{BC}\right\rVert_{1}\ . (90)
Proof.

We first note that by Hölder’s inequality and monotonicity of the trace norm for trace-preserving completely positive maps [31, Example 9.1.8 and Corollary 9.1.10] we have

|tr⁡(ΠBm⊗ΠCm​(ℛ⁡(ρB)−ℛ⁡(ΠBm​ρB​ΠBm)))|≤‖ℛ⁡(ρB)−ℛ⁡(ΠBm​ρB​ΠBm)‖1≤‖ρB−ΠBm​ρB​ΠBm‖1.\displaystyle\left|\mathrm{tr}\left(\Pi^{m}_{B}\otimes\Pi^{m}_{C}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(\rho_{B})-\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{B}^{m}\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})\bigr)\right)\right|\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{R}(\rho_{B})-\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{B}^{m}\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m})\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert\rho_{B}-\Pi_{B}^{m}\rho_{B}\Pi_{B}^{m}\right\rVert_{1}\ . (91)

Because the set of sub-normalized non-negative operators (i.e., the set of sub-normalized density operators) is complete99 9 We note that the set of sub-normalized density operators on a Hilbert space is clearly closed. Since every Hilbert space is complete and as every closed subspace of a complete space is complete [6, Chapter II, Section 3.4, Proposition 8] this implies that the set of sub-normalized density operators is complete., this sequence converges towards such an operator, i.e., we can define a density operator

Using the continuity of the fidelity (see, e.g., Lemma B.9 in [11]), this implies that

Δ¯ℛ​(ρ)=limm→∞Δ¯ℛ¯m​(ρ),\displaystyle\bar{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bar{\Delta}_{\bar{\mathcal{R}}^{m}}(\rho)\ , (109)

for any ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S}. Combining this with (100) gives

5 Proof of Corollary 2.4

The first statement of Corollary 2.4 that holds for separable Hilbert spaces follows immediately from Theorem 2.1, since 2−12I(A:C|B)ρ≥1−ln⁡(2)2I(A:C|B)ρ2^{-\frac{1}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}}\geq 1-\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}. The proof of the second statement of Corollary 2.4 is partitioned into three steps.1010 10 Although Corollary 2.4 does not immediately follow from Theorem 2.1 it is justified to term it as such, as it follows by the same proof technique that is used to derive Theorem 2.1 (in particular it makes use of Proposition 3.1). We first show that a similar method as used in Section 3 can be used to reveal certain insights about the structure of the recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} (which is not universal) that satisfies

F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))≥1−ln⁡(2)2I(A:C|B)ρ.\displaystyle F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\geq 1-\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\ . (111)

In a second step, by invoking Proposition 3.1, we use this knowledge to prove that for a fixed AA system there exists a recovery map that satisfies (111) which is universal and preserves the structure of the non-universal recovery map from before. Finally, in Step 3 we show how the dependency on the fixed AA system can be removed.

Step 1: Structure of a non-universal recovery map

We will show that for any density operator ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C, where AA, BB, and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces there exists a trace-preserving completely positive map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} that satisfies (111) and is of the form

XB↦ρB​C12​WB​C​(ρB−12​XB​ρB−12⊗idC)​WB​C†​ρB​C12,\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}W_{BC}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}X_{B}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})W_{BC}^{\dagger}\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}\ , (112)

on the support of ρB\rho_{B}, where WB​CW_{BC} is a unitary on B⊗CB\otimes C. We start by proving the following preparatory lemma.

Lemma 5.1.

For any density operator ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C, where AA, BB, and CC are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces there exists a trace-preserving completely positive map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} of the form

XB↦VB​C​ρB​C12​(ρB−12​UB​XB​UB†​ρB−12⊗idC)​ρB​C12​VB​C†,\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto V_{BC}\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}U_{B}X_{B}U_{B}^{\dagger}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}V_{BC}^{\dagger}\ , (113)

where VB​CV_{BC} is a unitary on B⊗CB\otimes C that commutes with ρB​C\rho_{BC} and UBU_{B} is a unitary on BB that commutes with ρB\rho_{B} such that

F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))≥1−ln⁡(2)2I(A:C|B)ρ.\displaystyle F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\geq 1-\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\ . (114)
Proof.

Let ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} be an arbitrary state on A⊗B⊗CA\otimes B\otimes C and let ρA​B​C0\rho^{0}_{ABC} be a Markov chain with the same marginal on the B⊗CB\otimes C system, i.e., ρB​C0=ρB​C\rho^{0}_{BC}=\rho_{BC}. For p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], define the state

ρA^​A​B​Cp:=(1−p)​|0⟩​⟨0|A^⊗ρA​B​C0+p|1⟩​⟨1|A^⊗ρA​B​C.\displaystyle\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}ABC}:=(1-p)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|_{\hat{A}}\otimes\rho^{0}_{ABC}+p|1\rangle\!\langle 1|_{\hat{A}}\otimes\rho_{ABC}\ . (115)

The main result of [11] (see Theorem 5.1 and Remark 4.3 in [11]) implies that there exists a recovery map ℛB→B​C\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC} of the form

XB↦VB​C​ρB​C12​(ρB−12​UB​XB​UB†​ρB−12⊗idC)​ρB​C12​VB​C†,\displaystyle X_{B}\mapsto V_{BC}\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}U_{B}X_{B}U_{B}^{\dagger}\rho_{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C})\rho_{BC}^{\frac{1}{2}}V_{BC}^{\dagger}\ , (116)

where UBU_{B} is diagonal with respect to the eigenbasis of ρB\rho_{B}, UB​UB†≤idBU_{B}U_{B}^{\dagger}\leq\mathrm{id}_{B} and VB​CV_{BC} is a unitary on B⊗CB\otimes C, such that

F(ρA^​A​B​Cp,ℛB→B​C(ρA^​A​Bp))≥1−ln⁡(2)2I(A^A:C|B)ρp.\displaystyle F\bigl(\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}AB})\bigr)\geq 1-\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(\hat{A}A:C|B)_{\rho^{p}}\ . (117)

By Lemma 5.2, using that I(A:C|B)ρ0=0I(A:C|B)_{\rho^{0}}=0 since ρA​B​C0\rho_{ABC}^{0} is a Markov chain, this may be rewritten as

p(1−F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B)))+(1−p)(1−F(ρA​B​C0,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B0)))≤pln⁡(2)2I(A:C|B)ρ.\displaystyle p\Bigl(1-F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)\Bigr)+(1-p)\Bigl(1-F\bigl(\rho^{0}_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho^{0}_{AB})\bigr)\Bigr)\leq p\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\ . (118)

Step 2: Structure of a universal recovery map for fixed AA system

In this step we show that the recovery map satisfying (111) of the form (112), whose existence has been established in Step 1, can be made universal without sacrificing the (partial) knowledge about its structure. The idea is to apply Proposition 3.1 for the function family

Δ~ℛ​(ρ):\displaystyle\tilde{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho):\,\,\,\, D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)→ℝ∪{−∞}\displaystyle\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}
ρA​B​C↦F(ρA​B​C,ℛB→B​C(ρA​B))−1+ln⁡(2)2I(A:C|B)ρ.\displaystyle\rho_{ABC}\mapsto F\bigl(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{B\to BC}(\rho_{AB})\bigr)-1+\frac{\ln(2)}{2}I(A:C|B)_{\rho}\ . (124)

We therefore need to verify that the assumptions of Proposition 3.1 are fulfilled. This is done by the following lemma. We first note that since CC is finite-dimensional this implies that Δ~ℛ​(ρ)<∞\tilde{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\rho)<\infty for all ρ∈D⁡(A⊗B⊗C)\rho\in\mathrm{D}(A\otimes B\otimes C).

Lemma 5.2.

Let AA be a separable and BB and CC finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The function family Δ~ℛ​(⋅)\tilde{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) defined by (124) satisfies Properties 1-4.

Proof.

We start by showing that Δ~ℛ​(⋅)\tilde{\Delta}_{\mathcal{R}}(\cdot) satisfies Property 1. For ρA^​A​B​Cp\rho^{p}_{\hat{A}ABC} as defined in (16), we have
